item.title: What is residual dizziness?
item.description: To help doctors better spot and manage BPPV-related RD, researchers have introduced an online decision-support tool called CLEAR (Clinician-Led Evaluation for Assessment of Residual Dizziness). Though this isn’t a treatment per se, it’s a structured way for clinicians to evaluate symptoms, consider risk factors, and plan appropriate follow-ups. This might include monitoring, referrals for vestibular rehabilitation therapy, or other strategies to support recovery and reduce the impact of dizzines

item.title: A Legacy of Research and Advocacy
item.description: More than a donor, Dr. Zee is a luminary whose work and generosity continue to steady our mission. His passion for clear diagnosis, scientific rigor, and patient-centered care inspires all of us. On behalf of VeDA and the broader vestibular community, we offer our heartfelt thanks today and for generations to come.

item.title: Memoir Writing Can Help Cope with Chronic Illness
item.description: When Kimberly Warner received unexpected news about the father who raised her, on top of being diagnosed with a chronic illness, she turned to writing to process her feelings. What came out was "Unfixed: A Memoir of Family, Mystery, and the Currents That Carry You Home", a haunting exploration of identity, loss, and the unsteady ground of becoming.

item.title: Ask Fiona: Understanding the Vestibular Nerve, Dizziness, and Body Triggers
item.description: Dizziness after recovery can still happen—and it doesn’t mean something is “wrong.”Even after a vestibular nerve injury heals, the brain can remain sensitive to certain positions, stress, or prolonged head/neck postures (like lying face down during a massage). Muscle tension, posture, and nervous system sensitivity can all trigger symptoms without re-injuring the nerve—and with the right strategies, this sensitivity often continues to improve over time.

item.title: A New Tool to Help Diagnose Vestibular Disorders
item.description: Researchers wanted to see if they could build a machine learning (ML) tool—a type of artificial intelligence—that could help doctors sort through the clues and narrow down the possibilities for six common vestibular disorders. item.title: Insights From the VeDA Registry
item.description: A new study in Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology reports important insights into the real-world experiences of people living with vestibular disorders based on data collected through a previous version of VeDA’s Patient Registry. item.title: Understanding Bilateral Vestibular Hypofunction
item.description: People living with bilateral vestibular hypofunction (BVH)—a condition in which the balance organs in both inner ears are damaged—often describe feeling unsteady, dizzy, or disconnected from their surroundings. A study by Dr. Andrew Wagner shows that a single test cannot capture the full picture of vestibular health for people with BVH.

item.title: Chronic vertigo & dizziness due to stroke
item.description: When people think about a stroke, many imagine sudden paralysis, facial drooping, and/or trouble speaking. However, other symptoms are often experienced and problematic — persistent vertigo and dizziness. These sensations are described as spinning (of the person or the environment), imbalance, or lightheadedness, and can linger for months or even years. item.title: Living Well with Chronic Vestibular Conditions
item.description: For many people, developing a vestibular disorder can feel like their life has been turned upside down.
